claims.statement: Koi Security reported that version 1.0.16 of the npm package postmark-mcp added a single line that copied every email sent through the MCP server to the publisher's own address, and called it the first malicious MCP server seen in the wild.
The package copied a legitimate postmark-mcp project hosted on GitHub; Postmark said the npm package was not official.
The malicious version was released on 17 September 2025; the package was later deleted from npm by its publisher after about 1,643 total downloads.
Koi described the package as downloaded about 1,500 times a week and integrated into hundreds of developer workflows.

unresolvedQuestions: Download figures differ by framing: about 1,500 a week (Koi, via SC Media) versus about 1,643 in total (The Hacker News). Keep both and attribute them.
The primary source is Koi's post as now hosted on the Palo Alto Networks blog after the Koi acquisition. Confirm the original koi.ai URL and publication date.
No named victim organization and no confirmed count of emails taken. Reviewer decides whether a single malicious package with no named victim fits the seed.
The researcher is now part of a vendor that sells a product for this risk. Don't treat the write-up as evidence that any product would have prevented it.

claims.statement: Koi Security audited the 2,857 skills then listed on ClawHub and found 341 malicious ones, 335 of them tied to one campaign it named ClawHavoc.
The ClawHavoc skills used fake prerequisite steps to get users to install the Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS).

Unit 42 reported that between February and May 2026 it found five further malicious ClawHub skills that had evaded blocking; OpenClaw banned the accounts and deleted the skills after Unit 42 reported them.

The Cloud Security Alliance describes ClawHub as a recurring supply-chain vector because OpenClaw grants installed skills broad local access, including credential stores, browser data and shell execution.
